item.title: Thousands swarm stunning mountain escape as selfie tourism backlash erupts online
item.description: Photos are showing massive shuttle lines at Tre Cime di Lavaredo in Italy as selfie tourism overwhelms one of the Dolomites' most iconic destinations for travelers.
item.content:encoded:
The pursuit of the perfect selfie is creating headaches for one of the Italian Alps' most recognizable landmarks.

Viral videos shared online in recent weeks show massive crowds stretching through shuttle queues as visitors wait to reach Tre Cime di Lavaredo, one of the most iconic destinations in Italy's Dolomites.

The videos have sparked outrage, with many online commenters arguing that visitors were more interested in taking photos than enjoying the mountains.

FAMOUS BEACH NOW REQUIRES VISITORS TO RESERVE SPOTS WEEKS AHEAD AND PAY FEES

"This video proves that people are no longer able to enjoy the journey," one commenter wrote on Instagram. "In their minds, the only thing that matters is the photo."

"Everyone lined up for a photo just to show people on social media how great their lives are," said another user. "Hours in line for one picture."

Tre Cime di Lavaredo is one of the most famous landmarks in the Dolomites. It draws visitors from around the world with its trio of mountain peaks.

The UNESCO-protected mountains are subject to the Enrosadira phenomenon, in which sunrise and sunset turn the rock walls a vibrant pink and orange, according to The Dolomites — UNESCO World Heritage Centre page. 

Tre Cime di Lavaredo gets over 800,000 visitors per year, per the Tre Cime di Lavaredo Hike Guide.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Hikers and climbers gravitate to legendary vertical rock faces in summer, while winter transforms the region into a massive and interconnected ski network, according to Dolomites.com.

In response to the growing crowds, officials are considering requiring reservations for shuttle passengers in addition to the reservation system already in place for drivers.

Drivers must reserve access to the Rifugio Auronzo parking area in advance, according to the reservation website.

Reservations cost €40 (about $45) for cars, €26 (about $30) for motorcycles and €60 (about $68) for camper vans.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Tre Cime is not the only destination in the Dolomites that's been grappling with issues caused by overtourism.

Landowners near Seceda, another popular mountain destination in the Dolomites, reinstated €5 (around $5.60) turnstiles to help manage growing crowds at one of the region's most photographed viewpoints, as Fox News Digital previously reported.

Carlo Zanella, president of the Alto Adige Alpine Club, previously told Fox News Digital that the turnstiles were installed by a local farmer after visitors repeatedly trampled meadows while flocking to the scenic overlook.

Zanella also criticized the role of social media in reshaping mountain tourism.

"I am against the influencers," he said. "They are only interested in making money [through] advertising."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Zanella encouraged visitors to explore lesser-known areas of the Dolomites, saying there are "other even more beautiful places to visit."

Ashley DiMella of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

item.title: Chevy Chase called out for being 'not so nice' to Billy Joel's ex-wife at a keg party
item.description: Katie Lee Biegel claimed on her podcast that Chevy Chase mistook her for staff and shooed her away at a keg party with her ex-husband Billy Joel.
item.content:encoded:
Billy Joel's ex-wife has called out Chevy Chase for being "not-so-nice" during an old-school keg party.

Katie Lee Biegel addressed the incident on a recent episode of her podcast, "All on the Table." She explained that the incident with Chase happened while she was married to Joel. The former couple tied the knot in 2004 before divorcing in 2009.

"My celebrity run-in that was not so nice was Chevy Chase," Biegel began.

"So, I was having a party with my ex-husband. It was a keg party. I wanted to have like an old-school keg party. We had a house that we were going to tear down. And it was like this little — we called it ‘The Sugar Shack,’ and had a very fun summer there, staying with friends," Biegel said.

JOEL MCHALE DISLOCATED CHEVY CHASE'S SHOULDER WHILE FILMING 'COMMUNITY'

She continued, "But then at the end of the summer, we decided to have a kind of like, ‘Tear the House Down' party, a keg party, and I had jello shots, kegs. It was a very star-studded party."

Biegel went on to explain the moment Chase mistook her for a member of the staff and "shooed" her away.

"And my ex-husband was standing talking to Chevy Chase and his wife. And I had a tray of jello shots. And I went up with the tray of jello shots and said, you know, ‘Do you guys want a shot?’ and Chevy thought that I was the staff at the party, and he took his hand and shooed me away," she said.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"He just did this," she said, making a shooing motion with her hand.

Chase has long had a reputation in Hollywood for being difficult to work with, with multiple former co-stars and collaborators alleging abrasive, confrontational and inappropriate behavior over the years.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

His most public controversies stem from his time on "Community," where he clashed with creator Dan Harmon and several cast members before leaving the show in 2012 after reportedly using racially insensitive language on set.

Fox News Digital reached out to Chase for comment.

item.title: Anthony Fauci diary entries set social media ablaze as critics mock, condemn behavior
item.description: Dr. Anthony Fauci's diary entries reveal his fixation on fame and media appearances during the COVID pandemic, sparking massive social media backlash.
item.content:encoded:
Once-private diary entries written by Dr. Anthony Fauci have set social media ablaze with critics mocking the former White House COVID advisor’s fixation on emerging from the global pandemic as a celebrity and condemning his behavior. 

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., made the diaries public as part of the committee's ongoing oversight investigation. The journals chronicle Fauci's day-to-day role during the COVID-19 crisis through conversations with President Donald Trump, governors and world leaders, while detailing his media appearances and personal observations. 

While much of the mainstream media initially ignored the shocking diary entries, there was no shortage of backlash on X. Outkick founder Clay Travis urged his followers to read the diary, calling Fauci "one of the true villains of American history." 

ABC, NBC, CBS, CNN AND MS NOW IGNORE FAUCI DIARY ENTRIES THAT REVEAL FIXATION ON FAME DURING COVID

Grabien Media founder Tom Elliott, who spent hours digging into the diary, found that the word "award" was mentioned 80 times, "hero" appeared 49 times, "press" appeared a staggering 641 times and Fauci never wrote anything about "peer review," "meta-analysis," "risk-benefit," "learning loss" or "mental health."

Dana Loesch was stunned, calling the diary "one of the most infuriating things I’ve ever read." 

Piers Morgan added, "These diaries are very damning. Fauci comes across as a fame-hungry narcissist who regularly said different things in private about Covid to what he told the world publicly."

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

Others put a spotlight on Fauci's apparent love for the TV camera. 

XX-XY founder Jennifer Sey unearthed an old Politico appearance in which Fauci simply read flattering tweets about himself. 

"Hard hitting stuff here," Sey snarked. "Could you kiss his butt anymore?"

FAUCI'S DIARY SHOWS HE FED QUESTIONS TO JOURNALISTS, BUILT FRIENDSHIPS WITH MEDIA FIGURES

Many comments were focused on Fauci's relationship with CNN anchor Jake Tapper, who appeared to be the doctor's closest media ally.  

The diary release came days before Fauci is scheduled to testify before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee after being subpoenaed by Paul, who also took to X to lampoon the diary. The senator shared an AI-generated image of Fauci sitting on a bed while writing in a diary. In the background are posters and toys in a humorous attempt to suggest the doctor was like a self-obsessed teenager. Next to the image, Paul wrote: "What Anthony Fauci looked like every night when he wrote about how great he is in his diary."

Fox News Digital reached out to Dr. Fauci and CNN for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Fox News Digital’s Amanda Macias contributed to this report.

item.title: Patriots receiver Mack Hollins’ barefoot escapades reach a new plateau in second New England season
item.description: Mack Hollins says New England restaurants now let him dine barefoot after his breakout Patriots season, but his shoeless habit is just one quirk.
item.content:encoded:
Mack Hollins has turned the proverbial corner as a New England Patriots wide receiver, but not in the ordinary way one might think, like his speed is improved or he reads defenders better now. This is more about his feet.

His habitually unapologetic bare feet.

Hollins reports that in his second year on the Patriots roster, his life habit of walking everywhere in his bare feet has gained acceptance locally. He knows this because restaurants are welcoming him in and allowing him to dine – sans shoes.

MACK HOLLINS ENTERS STADIUM WITH NO SHOES OR SHIRT

"I love it," Hollins told reporters at Patriots training camp during an interview session conducted barefoot. "It's really great because now they're kind of letting me slide being barefoot in restaurants and stuff because they know who I am.

"At first, it was like, some homeless guy coming in here, but now it's like the mechanic homeless guy so it's all right. So yeah, it's been great."

Let this marinate.

If you're pretty much disgusted by somebody else's bare feet on display anywhere but a beach, you're not going to be a fan. If you're thinking this is an attention-seeking move, well, maybe. Hollins has been known to stand out and not shy from attention.

ROB GRONKOWSKI OFFERS ADVICE FOR PATRIOTS TO SILENCE NOISE AROUND MIKE VRABEL CONTROVERSY AHEAD OF 2026 SEASON

But if you're a Patriots' fan and watched last season when Hollins unexpectedly started 13 regular-season games and two postseason games, and scored the team's only touchdown on a 35-yard reception in the Super Bowl LX, you might be more accepting of the guy's eccentricities.

And Hollins has a few.

He doesn't, for example, use forks or spoons or chopsticks or any other eating utensils. He uses his hands to eat because, he says, it helps him correctly gauge the temperature of the food which prepares his mouth for what's coming.

So, these New England restaurants are showing love to the barefoot guy who eats with his hands.

"Every team I've been on, you ask them who's the weirdest guy they're going to say Mack," Hollins once admitted.

But this isn't aloof weird.

Or disruptive weird.

It's perhaps endearing weird.

"Yeah, yeah, it's not like a bad weird," Hollins said.

It's weird like Hollins showing up to NFL games in Buffalo's frigid temperatures shirtless. Also barefoot, of course, despite the ice and snow on the ground.

It's weird like him arriving to the 2025 AFC Championship game between the Bills and Kansas City Chiefs wearing an Animal Muppet character — you know, the red thing that plays drums — mask.

All that aside, shoeless Mack Hollins is gaining traction in New England. And he has an explanation why he prefers to do without footgear when he's not actually in a game.

"I think shoes are a tool and people have made them a part of their body," Hollins once said. "I wouldn't walk around with a hammer just because I might need a hammer sometimes."

item.title: What a fourth-generation fishing captain has learned from nearly 100 years on the Gulf
item.description: Dylan Hubbard carries nearly 100 years of family legacy at Hubbard's Marina in Madeira Beach, navigating hurricanes, NOAA and a changing industry.
item.content:encoded:
For Dylan Hubbard, fishing is the easy part.

The harder part is carrying nearly 100 years of family history on his shoulders while figuring out how to keep the operation alive through hurricanes, federal regulators and a rapidly changing Florida tourism industry.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK

Hubbard is the fourth generation of his family to run Hubbard's Marina in Madeira Beach, Fla. The business traces its roots to 1928, when his grandfather started with five rowboats and 40 cane poles.

Today, Hubbard is vice president of the company and has begun the process of purchasing it from his father. But stepping into the family business was never as simple as inheriting a title.

"Oh, you have no idea," Hubbard told OutKick Outdoors when asked whether he had to earn his place before calling himself captain.

His grandfather, Wilson, originally ran the operation before leaving to serve during World War II. Hubbard's great-grandfather stepped in during that time, which is why the family considers it a fourth-generation business. His father later purchased the company from the family in 2004. Now, Dylan is preparing to carry it forward.

"It's also really cool to have that layer of: it's a family business. I'm fourth generation," Hubbard said. "Not only am I working, but also it's that legacy. So it's just an added layer of maybe responsibility or honor or blessing — whatever you want to call it — that really makes it even that much more special."

Watch Dylan Hubbard's full interview with OutKick Outdoors here:

That responsibility means knowing when to hold onto tradition and when to embrace change.

Hubbard's Marina began in Pass-a-Grille, back when Florida's barrier islands looked very different. But as new bridges changed traffic patterns and Pass-a-Grille became increasingly residential, Hubbard's grandfather recognized that the business needed a new home. Even though he was nearing 70 years old, he uprooted the operation and moved it north to John's Pass.

"He saw the writing on the wall," Hubbard said.

It was the kind of decision that probably felt risky at the time but proved essential in the decades that followed. John's Pass eventually developed into a major tourism destination, and Hubbard's grandfather also worked with the city to establish the boardwalk that now runs through the area.

That willingness to adapt has remained necessary — especially when nature delivered its worst, twice in less than two weeks.

In September 2024, Hurricane Helene brought nine feet of water into Hubbard's Marina. The main office was completely submerged, the main dock was destroyed, and the business lost infrastructure, inventory and equipment. Before the water had even fully receded, Hurricane Milton was bearing down as a Category 5, forcing the family to brace for a second direct hit while still standing in the wreckage of the first.

"It was pretty numbing," Hubbard said, "just a wild situation to go through."

Still, the boats survived. More importantly, so did the people.

Before official rescue crews could even reach the barrier islands, Hubbard and several crew members set out before daylight to assess the damage at John's Pass. What began as a trip to inspect the business quickly became something else entirely.

"We were the first boat out there," Hubbard said. "No one was out there — no fire, no EMS, no emergency folks. It was just us."

As they navigated through the damaged area, residents stood along seawalls crying, waving and begging for help. Some had stayed behind during the storm, become trapped, and then emerged to find they had lost everything.

"So what was supposed to be a search and find out what we needed to do and what got damaged turned into a rescue mission," Hubbard said.

Other members of the fishing community soon joined in, deploying their own boats to move people and supplies to and from the barrier islands — even as police tried, unsuccessfully, to keep boaters off the water given the debris and damage.

"We were essentially pirates for a week," he said.

For Hubbard, reopening quickly was never primarily about preserving the business's reputation or getting tourists back on boats. It was about his employees. At the time, the company had 84 staff members. Fifteen had lost everything in the storm.

"If I had just sat there and waited and not got to work, those people would not only have lost their homes and their vehicles and everything they owned, they would have also lost their jobs and not had income," Hubbard said. "So to me, it was imperative to open up as quickly as humanly possible."

The team rebuilt the dock in two days and had trips running again five days after Helene — faster than the barrier islands themselves officially reopened. The community later raised nearly $75,000 to help affected staff members.

In the year that followed, Hubbard's kept growing rather than pulling back: the company acquired a pirate ship, a dolphin tour boat and a shark tour operation in November 2025, adding to a portfolio that already includes a seafood market, a fuel dock and a boat-building operation. A new ghost tour just launched, and a Tampa Bay ferry service is next.

Capt. Hubbard may prefer being offshore, but much of his job now happens behind a desk, in meetings, or fighting battles that never make it onto a dock report.

Hubbard is heavily involved in fisheries management, serving as president of the Florida Guides Association and sitting on Gulf Council advisory panels covering reef fish, data collection and outreach.

A few years ago, that involvement got personal. After Hubbard publicly criticized weak enforcement against illegal charter operations at a federal meeting, NOAA's Office of Law Enforcement took a closer look at his own business — and told him the way Hubbard's Marina operated was against federal regulation.

It took him roughly 85 days to get the regulation itself changed, preserving his business model in the process.

"If you're not in the room, you're on the menu," Hubbard said of why he keeps showing up to meetings most people would find, in his words, "mind-numbing and boring."

CHARTER CAPTAIN JONATHAN MOSS EXPLAINS HOW TO GET KIDS HOOKED ON FISHING FROM AN EARLY AGE

It's not the only wild thing nearly 100 years on the Gulf has produced. Ask Hubbard for his strangest moment on the water and the answer comes without hesitation: "We've found dead bodies. We've come across boats on fire. We've saved people." His grandfather ran across great white sharks; his father, orcas; Hubbard himself has crossed paths with pilot whales, a right whale and one of the largest leatherback turtles he's ever seen.

"People always ask me, 'Do you still get to go fishing?'" Hubbard said. "I do, and I make time for it, and I definitely get out on the water as much as I can."

But he also understands that spending all his time fishing wouldn't necessarily serve the larger operation.

"If I spent my time offshore, that's definitely where I would rather be and enjoy a lot more," he said. "But I definitely wouldn't be in the position we are today if I did that all the time."

Hubbard hopes his grandfather would approve of where the family business stands today.

"I hope he would be happy," Hubbard said.

The pirate ship, the ferry, the federal meetings — none of that existed when Wilson Hubbard started with five rowboats. But the motto he built the business on hasn't changed.

"If you're too busy to go fishing, you're just too darn busy."

Still true, four generations later.

item.title: ESPN’s favorite insider accidentally explained why most Americans don’t trust the media
item.description: Andrew Marchand's defense of withholding the Ryan Clark story accidentally exposed how access journalism lets powerful people control the news cycle.
item.content:encoded:
"Write what you know, not what you think."

Andrew Marchand offered that lesson to other reporters while discussing ESPN’s decision to part ways with NFL analyst Ryan Clark. The sports-media columnist for The Athletic, a New York Times-owned outlet, was responding to what he described as inaccurate opinions circulating online about Clark’s dismissal.

He thought he was explaining the difference between responsible journalism and uninformed speculation. Instead, Marchand accidentally explained why so many Americans distrust the press.

ESPN PARTING WAYS WITH NFL ANALYST RYAN CLARK AHEAD OF NETWORK'S FIRST SUPER BOWL BROADCAST

To be clear, his advice was perfectly sound. The problem came when Marchand revealed what he knew, how long he had known it and why he had not told his readers.

On his own podcast, Marchand claimed he had anticipated Clark’s departure since February. He went so far as to assert that he had "a story prepared in February" and received a "very strong indication" roughly one week before ESPN let Clark go.

So why didn’t he publish the report?

"Like others, you want to allow ESPN to tell him first," Marchand explained. He said he eventually reported that Clark was expected to be dismissed because the scoop became "competitive."

In other words, Marchand says he knew ESPN was preparing to part ways with Clark but he withheld the information while ESPN followed its preferred timetable. Then another outlet threatened to make the information public, and he published.

Marchand apparently believed that account enhanced his reputation as a responsible journalist.

It actually exposed the access-journalism game.

Before going further, it's important to make clear that the point is not Marchand personally, or who published one Ryan Clark story first.

Legendary sports radio host Dan Patrick recently brought up another situation that exposed why access-journalism serves the people involved, but often not the public at large.

After the San Francisco 49ers disclosed that head coach Kyle Shanahan had suffered serious injuries in a car accident 11 days earlier, ESPN’s Adam Schefter posted the news one minute later. ESPN quickly followed with a detailed report.

Patrick wondered whether ESPN and Schefter already knew what had happened but waited until the 49ers authorized its release.

"This isn’t journalism. Not really reporting," Patrick said. "They’re giving you the information" and then effectively saying, "Okay, now you can tell everybody."

Patrick didn't prove ESPN had been sitting on the story. But he identified the central problem with the modern insider economy: What is the public value of privately knowing something if the institution involved decides when the public may know it?

That's not journalism. It's public relations.

And while we don't know exactly what happened between Schefter, Kyle Shanahan, ESPN, the NFL and the San Francisco 49ers, we do know exactly how the Marchand-Clark situation played out and it illustrates Patrick's point.

As I detailed last week, my colleague Bobby Burack and I developed separate lines of reporting that ESPN was preparing to part ways with Clark. Four sources in total confirmed the information.

We contacted ESPN at 4 p.m. ET on Monday and gave the network until 5 to respond. ESPN asked us to delay publication until 5:45 while it was "trying to chase this down." We declined but offered to add anything the network provided.

Clark then disappeared from "NFL Live," ESPN unexpectedly told us at 4:49 that we could "stick to" our original timeline, and Marchand published a two-paragraph report 14 minutes later. OutKick’s more detailed story followed one minute after that.

That looks damning because it appears Marchand rushed out a short and incomplete story just to beat OutKick to the news.

Marchand has now explained his side, and his explanation makes the sequence harder to defend.

Recall that Marchand claimed he had "a story prepared in February." But his initial report didn't resemble a completed article that had been waiting since February. It consisted of two hurried paragraphs and included a typo.

Whatever "prepared" meant, his comments in a separate interview with Puck’s John Ourand established the more important point: Marchand had the information, intentionally waited on ESPN and published only after OutKick’s reporting forced the company to act.

"ESPN knew, I knew," Marchand told Ourand, explaining that the network had been trying to keep the Clark decision "close to the vest."

Then, Marchand said, "another entity called up" with the information and informed ESPN that it intended to publish. According to Marchand, ESPN became concerned and decided to tell Clark immediately rather than risk having him learn about the decision online.

CNN PANELIST BLAMES 'CULTURE WAR' RETRIBUTION AS REASON FOR RYAN CLARK'S ESPN DEPARTURE

Marchand didn't identify the other outlet, but he was describing precisely what OutKick had done. Our inquiry didn't merely make the story abstractly "competitive." By Marchand’s own account, it forced ESPN to accelerate its timetable.

Once ESPN had informed Clark, Marchand rushed out his two-paragraph report and made sure to note afterward that he had "reported it first," while the other outlet published "a little bit after."

Marchand didn't explain who alerted him that OutKick was preparing to publish or who told him Clark had been informed. Nor does his account prove ESPN asked us to wait specifically to help another reporter publish first.

And there is nothing inherently improper about giving a company a brief opportunity to notify an employee before he learns online that he has been let go. Reporters should consider the human consequences of publication.

But Marchand didn't describe granting ESPN a few minutes of courtesy. He said he possessed strong information for roughly a week and waited until competition threatened the arrangement.

Marchand went further in his interview with Ourand. He described himself as "being respectful" by waiting for ESPN and said he tries to wait "as long as you can" before publishing layoff news.

He then suggested that being a good reporter and being a good person "go hand-in-hand."

Marchand isn't simply admitting that he honored ESPN’s timetable. He is presenting that deference as evidence of his moral and journalistic superiority.

But OutKick didn't recklessly publish unconfirmed information or deny ESPN an opportunity to respond. We independently confirmed the story through four sources, contacted the company and gave it a firm deadline.

Marchand’s definition of responsible journalism appears to require something more: allowing the corporation at the center of the story to determine when the reporting may become public.

Responsible journalism means giving the subject of a story an opportunity to respond, as OutKick did when we offered ESPN one hour to comment.

But it does not mean giving the subject control over when the story becomes public. And it especially doesn't mean allowing the subject to dictate the framing of the news.

That's the difference between responsible journalism and access journalism. It seems that Marchand and many other insiders confuse the two quite frequently.

Access reporters receive strategically selected information from powerful sources, honor the source’s preferred timetable and publish when the institution decides the information can be released.

The reporter receives exclusives and status. The institution receives a predictable messenger.

Marchand demonstrated that predictability during the interview with Ourand.

Although he called ESPN’s execution "horrendous," he repeatedly insisted the company was "trying to do the right thing" and that its "hearts were in the right place."

ESPN put Clark on live television despite planning to part ways with him, removed him only after an outside outlet threatened to publish and created the humiliating spectacle Marchand was discussing.

Yet even while criticizing the result, a reporter who benefits from staying in ESPN’s good graces rushed to defend management’s intentions. The execution was bad, Marchand conceded, but ESPN’s motives, in his view, remained pure.

That instinct points to the second half of the access bargain. It's not only about allowing a source to control the timing of information. It's also about how aggressively a reporter is willing to scrutinize the people providing it.

A reporter who depends on one corporation for a steady stream of scoops has a powerful incentive not to challenge that corporation too aggressively. The next exclusive depends on the same executives and communications officials continuing to take his calls.

Marchand does criticize people associated with ESPN. But notice who draws his criticism and when they draw it.

His most sustained criticism has focused on Pat McAfee, an independently powerful personality whom ESPN does not fully control and who has repeatedly clashed with people inside the network. One Marchand report contained several petty and embarrassing details about McAfee that clearly came from ESPN insiders. Sports Illustrated described it as a "pretty brutal inside job."

That was technically reporting critical of an ESPN personality. It also demonstrated how an insider can serve one faction of a corporation against another.

Marchand criticized Ryan Clark after ESPN had decided to fire him. He wrote that "Around the Horn" had lost its way during the show’s final week, months after ESPN publicly announced its cancellation.

Even Marchand and Katie Strang’s substantial investigation into former ESPN executive Lee Fitting arrived after ESPN had let him go, when scrutinizing Fitting no longer threatened his standing inside the network. The report documented conduct that employees said went unchecked for years, but its target was already outside the building.

The discarded executive received scrutiny. The executives who still controlled access received credit.

That doesn't prove a formal quid pro quo. But it doesn't need to.

The institution supplies information. The reporter supplies predictability and favorable coverage.

The same arrangement becomes far more consequential when the subject is not a sports network but a government official helping shape national policy.

Newly released diary entries from Dr. Anthony Fauci showed just how cozy relationships between powerful officials and the journalists covering them can become.

Fauci wrote that he was building a friendship with CNN’s Jake Tapper and documented dinners at each other’s homes. He wrote that he "gave Jake some questions to ask" another health official during a CNN interview.

Dana Bash sent Fauci an encouraging message after a confrontation with a Republican lawmaker. George Stephanopoulos praised Fauci privately after an interview, while Andrea Mitchell called to apologize for failing to book him.

Reporters need sources, and friendly relationships can produce important information. None of those described interactions is a problem in a vacuum.

The problem arises when access, ideological sympathy and personal friendship erase the necessary distance between reporter and subject.

During a historic public-health crisis, the press was supposed to scrutinize one of the most powerful and influential officials in the country. Fauci’s diaries raise a different possibility: that some journalists covering him had begun to view him less as a subject requiring skepticism and more as an ally whose access and approval they valued.

INSIDE FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY: WHAT HE WROTE ABOUT TRUMP, TV PERSONALITIES AND CELEBRITIES

The Marchand-ESPN sequence shows the access bargain in sports media. The Fauci diaries show what happens when that same bargain reaches national policy.

That's the access bargain in its most dangerous form.

The information can be accurate and still function as PR. It can be selectively leaked, strategically timed and framed to benefit the institution or official providing it.

That's why many insider scoops provide limited public value. Firings, trades, contract extensions and television assignments generally become public anyway. The insider’s product is often not discovery, it's speed.

And in today's social media world, how much value does that even hold?

The Founding Fathers didn't enshrine freedom of the press in the First Amendment so reporters could distribute corporate announcements a few minutes early or launder government messaging from powerful officials.

They protected it because a free press was supposed to stand between the public and concentrated power.

That freedom carries a purpose: expose what powerful institutions want concealed, demand answers they would rather avoid and publish truths they would prefer remain buried.

When reporters instead allow corporations and government officials to control the timing, framing and scrutiny of the news, they are not fulfilling that founding role.

They are surrendering it.

My own career has often involved seeking access where I was not wanted. Nike stonewalled questions about a study on "transgender" youth athletes, the WNBA denied game credentials several times because they didn't want me asking questions and reporting on a Michigan high-school volleyball controversy led to harassment and required me to have a personal security detail at several games.

OUTKICK REPORTER HARASSED COVERING GIRLS VOLLEYBALL, TRANS PLAYER, AS PRINCIPAL DOES NOTHING

That resistance didn't make all of my conclusions correct, but it established that the subjects weren't controlling the reporting process. Quite the opposite, in fact.

Only 28% of Americans told Gallup last year that they trusted newspapers, television and radio to report the news fully, accurately and fairly, the lowest figure Gallup has recorded.

Media organizations often blame polarization, misinformation, social media and politicians for that collapse.

They should also examine the system they created.

Marchand thought he was establishing his superiority over reporters who lacked his access. He knew earlier, had better sources, supposedly had a story ready months before and then simply waited because that was the "responsible" thing to do.

Instead, his defense revealed the unspoken arrangement.

A powerful institution gives information to a favored reporter. The reporter protects the institution’s timeline and rarely makes himself a threat to the people providing access. When an outside outlet disrupts the arrangement, the insider rushes out the news, preserves his reputation and continues receiving information from the same sources.

Then he lectures everyone else to "write what you know, not what you think."

Marchand should add the unofficial second half of that rule: Write what you know... as long as the corporation that told you says it is okay.

Dan Patrick identified the problem.

Andrew Marchand accidentally showed the entire process in action.

item.title: House committee passes Foreign Funding Transparency Act to expose foreign donations to nonprofits
item.description: The Foreign Funding Transparency Act targets foreign nationals funneling money through tax-exempt organizations to political committees in the U.S.
item.content:encoded:
Lawmakers are seeking to expose foreign nationals who may be funneling money and donations through tax-exempt organizations to political committees as the House Ways and Means Committee passed a bill that would revise reporting requirements for tax-exempt groups.

The Foreign Funding Transparency Act, which passed 23-18 in the committee last Wednesday, would require tax-exempt organizations to collect and report to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) donations received from foreign nationals.

"For far too long, foreign influence and interference have plagued our tax-exempt sector," committee Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., said in a statement. "Foreign donations have no place in American politics, particularly when the sole goal is to manipulate our public discourse, promote propaganda and support violence."

Smith noted that many of the protests and demonstrations that take place across the U.S. appear to be grassroots but are actually well-organized and well-funded, often by groups within what he described as "shadowy networks."

"As the Ways and Means Committee conducted its investigation into the nation’s tax-exempt sector, it became clear that shadowy networks of well-funded organizations have been enjoying lucrative tax benefits for decades, while simultaneously accepting donations and direction from foreign nationals," Smith added. "From the outside, it looks like a movement, but once you see how the money flows, it becomes clear that this is a machine," he added. 

The bill’s passage came just a week after Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for global cooperation at a summit in Washington to combat far-left political terrorism.

SHANGHAI SABOTAGE: INSIDE SINGHAM'S SECRET STRATEGY TO DEMONIZE AMERICA

"For far too long, however, our counterterrorism doctrine has had a blind spot – a blind spot when it comes to extremist violence from the political left," Rubio said. "Even today, the very idea that far-left terrorism could be a serious threat is treated as a right-wing fever dream, or worse, as a dangerous fascist conspiracy."

While Rubio didn’t mention any organizations or individuals by name, the House Ways and Means Committee noted Marxist Neville Roy Singham in a statement about the bill’s passage.

Singham, a 72-year-old American now based in Shanghai and who sold his tech company for $785 million in 2017, is known to fund pro-Chinese Communist Party groups operating in the U.S. He has funneled $278 million into the broad network of nonprofits since 2017, according to a Fox News Digital investigation.

The funneling of funds through nonprofit networks has been a key point of concern for lawmakers and the Trump administration. Major contributors, including Singham, often have dispersed funds through shell 501(c)(3) nonprofits, which subsequently contributed to various tax-exempt organizations.

RUBIO'S CALL TO COMBAT GLOBAL FUNDERS OF FAR-LEFT TERRORISM COULD PUT SINGHAM IN CROSSHAIRS

During his address to more than 60 countries earlier this month, Rubio noted that networks have been coordinating across multiple countries, providing training instructions and using encrypted communication to facilitate unrest. He said international cooperation was critical to disrupting the financing of dangerous organizations, some of which were working with hostile foreign states.

Singham did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

item.title: Kaylee Goncalves' mother says family ready for trial after Bryan Kohberger seeks to withdraw guilty plea
item.description: Kaylee Goncalves' mother says the family is confident in the evidence and hopes a trial would lead to a death penalty conviction for Bryan Kohberger.
item.content:encoded:
Idaho student killer Bryan Kohberger is seeking to withdraw his guilty plea in a bid for a trial, but the family of victim Kaylee Goncalves says they're ready if he gets his wish.

"We knew we'd be hearing from him again, and September was coming up and that would be the end of his appeal, so we weren't really shocked," Kristi Goncalves, Kaylee's mother, said Monday.

Speaking with Fox News' Sean Hannity, Goncalves said her family has remained confident in the overwhelming evidence against Kohberger and would welcome the opportunity to present the case before a jury.

IDAHO MURDERS: NEW BOOK ON KOHBERGER REVEALS PREVIOUSLY UNSEEN EVIDENCE, CLAIMS SHEATH COULD BE INADMISSIBLE

"Honestly, either way this goes, whether the judge dismisses it right out the gate, fantastic, or if we wind up in court, we still feel like we wanted to go [to trial] in the first place," she said.

"We are very confident in the evidence in this case and, hopefully, if we do go to trial this time, he will be convicted and sentenced to death."

Kohberger, 31, pleaded guilty to murdering four University of Idaho students last year and was sentenced to four consecutive life sentences.

BRYAN KOHBERGER'S MOTHER CALLED HIM 'MY ANGEL' AND INSISTED POLICE MADE A 'REALLY, REALLY BAD MISTAKE': BOOK

Court records show that he filed a handwritten petition for post-conviction relief Monday. In the petition, Kohberger argued that he was "convinced to falsely confess," claiming his high-profile defense team of Anne Taylor, Elisa Massoth and Bicka Barlow didn't tell him about "exculpatory discovery" — evidence mentioned in the recent "Broken Plea" book but never vetted in court.

The news circulated after Kohberger called a New York Times reporter and claimed that he has an "absolute claim of innocence."

Reacting to the petition, former prosecutor and "Crime Stories" host Nancy Grace said Kohberger's effort to undo his plea deal should be met with exactly what he is asking for.

"Bring it on," Grace said on "Hannity."

"I agree with one thing Bryan Kohberger said in his self-styled petition. He says justice was not served. And amen, brother. It was not served because he needs the death penalty."

Fox News Digital's Michael Ruiz contributed to this report.

item.title: Tick Tock: SEC and Big Ten receive revised Protect College Sports Act as Senate vote timeline looms
item.description: Revised Protect College Sports Act language was sent to SEC and Big Ten for opinion after weeks of work from Ted Cruz, Maria Cantwell and other leaders.
item.content:encoded:
It's been a long process, but revisions to the 'Protect College Sports Act' have been sent to conference commissioners for their approval after immense pressure over the past month.

Last week, Senate Majority Leader John Thune throwing doubt into a vote happening on the legislation essentially stoked a fire with Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) to get this bill in a form in which it could possibly be taken to the Senate floor.

Now, we have entered goal line territory.

The bipartisan bill was created to help navigate college athletics in this messy time, and out of courtrooms, with numerous eligibility lawsuits filed within the past week alone.

Running out of time: SEC, Big Ten wait on 'Protect College Sports Act' revisions as August recess nears

After years of lobbying Congress for help, which led to the SCORE Act being created before this latest bill, there is a growing dissension between parties on how much actual help is wanted at the federal level.

The biggest hurdle for this legislation was getting the support of conferences like the SEC and Big Ten, who have been holding out on giving their approval until certain sections of the bill were to their liking, or at least did not present hurdles that were too far gone for agreement.

On Sunday night, and into early Monday morning, officials from multiple conferences were holding calls with both Cantwell and Cruz. In addition, multiple members of President Trump's committee on saving college athletics were on these calls, hoping to help the revision process.

Last week during SEC Media Days, commissioner Greg Sankey mentioned to OutKick-FOX News that there needed to be certain areas of the legislation tied up so there would not be any loopholes that needed to be corrected, if the bill were to be voted on and signed into law.

"I think the reality is, if a bill is produced and advances, and it's eventually signed into law, the view will be we've solved those problems," Sankey mentioned. "And, Congress is going to move onto taxation, funding whatever, international issues. You just make a list, they have a lot of important issues, and they’re not coming back to close gaps or solve problems.

GREG SANKEY ADDRESSES SEC BREAKAWAY TALK AS MICHIGAN TRIES TO STEAL SPOTLIGHT WITH AD WARDE MANUEL DECISION

"That's why since the act was introduced, we've been focused on common sense adjustments to close the loopholes and make this manageable. There's energy and effort in that, but that doesn’t mean we're at the finish line yet."

Big Ten commissioner had this to say about the substance of the Protect College Sports Act

"We preferred a much skinnier bill than this bill," Petitti said. "That is not the reality right now. So we have to work within the framework of what's happening and make decisions about it as a totality..I frame the question as 'is there more good here than not?'. That's the way to look at it."

In terms of the revised bill, sources tell OutKick-FOX News that given the new language presented, this could be a landmark moment in college athletics.

"The ball has been punted to the Big Ten and SEC, so it will now be interesting to see how they approach this moving forward. They (congressional leaders) are working on a timeline here, and if something is going to be voted on, it's time," a source told OutKick-FOX News.

One of the bigger issues centered around whether conferences like the Big Ten and SEC could increase their member institutions. The summary, which OutKick-FOX News obtained, does not mention a cap on how many schools each conference can add in the future.

"I don't think anybody expects that we get the changes and just check the box. It's all good. There's going to be back and forth, there's still work to do..We'll go as fast as we can....We sent comments back to the Senators on July third," Big Ten commissioner Tony Petitti said Tuesday.

It should be noted that there are issues that have already been discussed by all parties that were not included in the summary, like conferences having a cap put on how many schools can be added in the form of expansion.

According to sources familiar with the ongoing discussions, here were the concessions made to the SEC and Big Ten around the PCSA.

Looking at these concessions, compared to the previous legislation, here's where both conferences did not get what they wanted.

Essentially, the Big Ten and SEC got a very large chunk of what they wanted with these revisions, with final language being discussed throughout the next few days.

In the revisions, with some conferences hitting back on how much money is being spent on retaining players compared to the financials spent on the transfer portal and even high school recruiting, Senators worked in a part in which there would now be a separate salary pool for keeping players on current rosters.

The SEC and Big Ten were not prepared to comment publicly on the matter until they were able to look at the entire bill.

Well, now comes the waiting game.

Officials from the Big Ten and SEC are going to have their lawyers look over the revisions to see if they are in large-part what they were hoping for. If they were to approve of these changes, then you would see both conferences come out in support of the legislation, along with Presidents and Chancellors from member schools.

If they do not support these revisions fully, then Senators Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) would try and push this to the Senate floor without their support. The problem lies in where does a majority of their support come from with this bill.

There are a number of Senators who do no support the legislation, with a list that also includes the National Black Caucus.

Can this pass without their support? Possibly, but having a bill pass with just enough votes is in a whole different ballpark than it passing with flying colors.

For now, the waiting game continues, with the Big Ten taking centerstage this week, though they are in constant communication with the SEC.

Here we go. If this is going to happen, we are officially in 3rd or 4th down territory.

item.title: Kansas teacher says she'll continue using students' preferred pronouns as district faces federal investigation
item.description: A Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools teacher says she will keep using students' preferred names and pronouns despite a federal investigation.
item.content:encoded:
A Kansas teacher says she will continue using students' preferred names and pronouns despite an ongoing federal investigation into her school district's gender identity policies, drawing renewed attention to the district's approach to parental notification and student records.

"I am a teacher in USD 500," Courtney Richardson, a teacher at Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools, wrote in a Friday post on Facebook. "I am a PROUD 🌈 ally in all of the spaces that I am in. If your child was born Nicole, and one day they ask me to call them Nick so they feel more comfortable, then I am going to call them Nick and keep it moving. That is not indoctrination. That is a teacher being a safe place for ALL kids. Period."

On the Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools website, Richardson appears to be listed as a science teacher.

TRUMP ADMIN TARGETS WOKE SCHOOLS ACCUSED OF HIDING STUDENTS' GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS

"Yall want me to call to ask your permission first," she asked. "Funny thing, when I call home about grades and behaviors, parents seldom answer or respond to messages. So we care more about Nicole being called Nick than we care about￼ these kids graduating without being able to read at grade level, or to form a thought without ChatGPT?! Has anyone of you people who are so passionate about pronouns ever shown up and supported these kids in these schools? The stands at basketball games, music concerts, NHS ceremonies, and PTA meetings are empty, yet yall packed out the board meeting over teachers allegedly not notifying parents of their child’s preferred pronouns?"

On her LinkedIn page, Richardson says she has worked at Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools as a teacher full-time from July 2019 to the present.

She listed one of her past positions as a full-time community organizer for the Kansas Democratic Party in 2018.

RAHM EMANUEL SPARS WITH NEW YORKER INTERVIEWER WHO GRILLED HIM FOR NOT EMPHASIZING TRANS ISSUES

Richardson continued, "I mean the bigger problem is that your kids don’t feel comfortable enough talking to you, their parents, about this. 🗣️THAT SAYS MORE ABOUT YOU FAILING AS A PARENT THAN IT DOES ABOUT US 🌈 SUPPORTERS!!!!! I will continue to be a safe place for all who enter my space. Y’all are weirdos. Thank you for subscribing to my TedTalk."

In a follow-up comment on her post, which received over 100 comments and over 300 reactions, Richardson wrote, "Also, I didn’t say anything wrong, so I fear no consequences. 💅🏾 I don’t care who screenshots this."

At the beginning of the month, the Trump administration said it was considering taking enforcement action against Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools, including potentially withholding federal funding, over policies it says do not require school staff to inform parents when a student identifies as transgender.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION OPENS FOUR TITLE IX INVESTIGATIONS INTO MICHIGAN AND NORTH CAROLINA SCHOOL DISTRICTS

The Education Department said the district's policy of not informing parents about a student's transgender status violates the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, and said it is working with the Justice Department on possible enforcement actions, which could include litigation and the loss of federal funding.

In a press release, the Department of Education stated, "The Trump Administration’s policy is simple: the blatant refusal to acknowledge parental rights will not be tolerated."  

A spokesperson for Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools told Fox News Digital in a statement, "Since this is a personnel matter, KCKPS can not comment at this time."

Fox News Digital reached out to Richardson for comment but did not immediately hear back.

item.title: Millions could gain easier access to popular peptides after FDA panel vote
item.description: An FDA panel voted to recommend six peptides including BPC-157, TB-500, and KPV for compounding by licensed pharmacies instead of grey market vendors.
item.content:encoded:
An FDA advisory committee has voted by a majority to recommend broader access to certain peptides.

Peptides are short chains of amino acids that help regulate functions such as metabolism, growth and tissue repair, according to Cleveland Clinic.

Some peptides are used in FDA-approved medications, including insulin and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, while others are experimental compounds marketed for wellness or performance that remain under federal review.

FDA TO REVIEW 7 POPULAR PEPTIDES TOUTED FOR WEIGHT LOSS, HEALING AND LONGEVITY

Seven peptides were reviewed during a two-day hearing held by the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee in Maryland last week. The panel considered whether each peptide should be added to the Section 503A Bulks List.

If ultimately approved by the FDA, licensed compounding pharmacies could prepare them for valid prescriptions instead of leaving patients to rely on unregulated online vendors.

The committee voted in favor of loosening restrictions on the following six peptides, according to Reuters.

While some peptide experts celebrate this as one step closer to access to life-improving drugs, others claim there isn’t enough data on safety and efficacy. The FDA will now consider the committee's recommendation before making a final decision.

Jim LaValle, a Texas-based clinical pharmacist and chair of the International Peptide Society, who testified at the hearings, noted that restrictions still exist.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"This was not FDA approval, nor was it a blanket endorsement of every peptide, every use or unrestricted access," LaValle, who is also a board-certified nutritionist, told Fox News Digital. "I have said throughout this process that you do not solve a quality problem by forcing the market underground."

"I was encouraged by the committee’s recommendation because it creates an opportunity to move patients away from unverified research use only (RUO), otherwise known as grey market products, and toward a more accountable medical pathway."

LaValle said his work with the International Peptide Society focuses on training clinicians about the potential benefits and risks of peptide therapies as interest in the compounds grows.

The "right model" is access with guardrails, qualified clinicians, licensed pharmacies, validated quality testing and "meaningful" patient follow-up, according to the expert.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"My hope is that the FDA follows the recommendation with a transparent, science-driven process; establishes clear, peptide-specific standards; and follows the guidance for approving a substance that meets the FDA’s current regulations," LaValle said.

This process includes checking that both the active ingredient and the final product meet quality standards, and setting up a system for tracking and reporting any side effects.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"The peptide revolution is here," LaValle said. "However, don’t expect miracles. Better choices related to diet, exercise, gut health, sleep, stress and managing metabolic health, guided by regular lab assessments, should be the goal."

"In some cases, peptides can play an important part on the journey of performance aging and repair," he went on. "The American public should understand that nothing changed overnight."

LaValle emphasized that the advisory committee's vote was only a recommendation, not a final FDA decision, and noted that compounded medications are regulated differently than FDA-approved drugs.

"The evidence is also not equally mature across all peptides that are approved by the FDA," he noted. "People should avoid products sold online as ‘research use only’ and should not self-experiment."

"Any consideration of peptide therapy should involve a qualified licensed clinician and a legitimate licensed pharmacy."

item.title: IndyCar unveils new car coming in 2028 to replace current generation after 15-year-run
item.description: The IR-28 chassis brings a lighter design, twin-turbo V6 engines, and enhanced hybrid powertrain to IndyCar after 15 years with the same car.
item.content:encoded:
While there have been some big technological and safety enhancements over the years, the NTT IndyCar has been using the same cars for nearly fifteen years.

But in 2028, the series' cars are finally getting a long-awaited refresh with the IR-28 chassis, which was unveiled on Tuesday.

And it's a beaut, Clark.

While the IndyCar DNA is still very apparent — which is what we all want — this chassis takes some steps into the future compared to the current DW12, which debuted in 2012.

Twenty. Twelve.

That's an eternity in motorsports. For comparison, the NASCAR Cup Series refreshed its cars twice in that span, Formula 1 has done it three times, and Formula E (which only debuted in 2014) is slated to introduce four cars later this year.

INDYCAR TEAMS COME TO TERMS ON THE SERIES' FIRST-EVER CHARTER SALE, WHICH SHAKES UP THE GRID FOR 2027

So, yeah, it's time.

This chassis is the first to be designed with two big IndyCar additions — the Aeroscreen and hybrid powertrains — in mind, and is expected to be around 100 pounds lighter than its predecessor.

The IR-28 features new front and rear wings for both superspeedways and road and street courses, with the new aero package being designed to allow for closer racing.

TRUMP TOUTS INDYCAR DRIVERS' 'SPECIAL' ABILITY AT FREEDOM 250 GRAND PRIX SHOWCASE, SEEMINGLY ENDING HOT DEBATE

The engine cover will give some real estate to the engine manufacturers, and the overall body design allows for more sponsorship space.

Speaking of engines, Honda and Chevrolet will continue on as engine suppliers under the new formula, which will introduce 2.4-liter twin-turbocharged V6 engines that can produce up to 760 horsepower.

The series will introduce a new hybrid system that uses a battery-based Energy Storage System (ESS) with an estimated 14 times the storage capacity of the current system.

It sounds like a solid recipe, and reigning four-time series champion Alex Palou concurs.

"Seeing the car for the first time made me even more excited about where IndyCar is going," Palou said. "The design is super cool and feels like a proper next step for the series while still looking like an IndyCar Series car."

While there's a lot of excitement for the future, drivers still have to focus on this season, including a busy final stretch of the season.

The series heads to Portland International Raceway on August 9, then the Streets of Markham, Ontario on August 16.

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington, DC will take place on August 23, followed by a doubleheader at the Milwaukee Mile on August 29 and 30. The season finale will be on September 6 at WeatherTech Raceway Laguna Seca.

Ryan Lasko, the No. 18 prospect for the Athletics, is improving after fracturing his C6-C7 vertebrae.

Lasko suffered the injury during a horrific collision in a game earlier this month. While playing center field for Double-A Midland, Lasko and right fielder Devin Taylor collided while going for a ball in the gap.

METS TROT OUT A KOREAN POP STAR WITH AN AMAZING WINDUP FOR FIRST PITCH DUTIES, WEMBY PLAYS SOCCER & ROSIE

"I'm very happy with my progress and once again, so thankful for all the love and support. It has continued to help me get up every day and work my hardest," he added.

Lasko is one of the Athletics’ top prospects, entering the season as the franchise’s No. 18 prospect, per MLB Pipeline. He was taken by the Athletics in the 2023 MLB Draft in the second round.

item.title: WATCH: US envoy defends walkout during France's 'condescending' remarks, vows boycott
item.description: Dan Negrea accused France of "disingenuous grandstanding" and vowed American diplomats will keep walking out during French statements at the U.N.
item.content:encoded:
The United States dramatically walked out as France addressed the United Nations (U.N.) Security Council Monday, escalating an extraordinary clash between the longtime allies after Paris claimed America was no longer a "beacon of human rights."

The U.S. delegation left the chamber as French Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont delivered remarks during a Security Council meeting on Ukraine, days after France’s U.N. mission in Geneva accused Washington of standing alongside North Korea, Nicaragua, Mali and Russia following a vote on the U.N.’s human rights chief.

Deputy U.S. Ambassador Dan Negrea accused France of "disingenuous grandstanding" and warned that American diplomats would continue walking out during French statements until Paris renounces what he called its "condescending and disrespectful rhetoric."

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TOUTS MORE THAN $1B IN UN BUDGET CUTS AS REFORM PUSH GAINS MOMENTUM

"Today, I remind them that it is the United States that remains the beacon of liberty for the world," Negrea told the council. "As such, we will not be affording them the benefit of listening to their politicized drivel until they renounce their condescending and disrespectful rhetoric and behave in a manner commensurate with their seat on this council."

The clash matters because the United States and France are among the world’s oldest allies, dating back to French support for the American Revolution, and today remain NATO partners and permanent members of the U.N. Security Council. Their cooperation is central to Western policy on Ukraine, European security and sanctions enforcement.

A French diplomat told Fox News Digital that the dispute should not be interpreted as a broader rupture between the longtime allies. "Differences in how we assess a vote do not call into question the quality of our relations or our ability to work together," the diplomat said.

Israel’s U.N. Ambassador Danny Danon backed Washington’s response and sharply criticized France.

"I think the behavior of France is shameful," Danon told Fox News Digital Tuesday. "The U.S. is demonstrating moral clarity, standing for the real values of the U.N."

Danon accused France and other European countries of supporting voices within the United Nations that undermine rather than advance human rights. "It’s about time to reform the U.N., and I want to thank the U.S. for showing leadership on that issue," he said.

The confrontation marked a significant escalation from the unusually personal social media exchange that erupted after the General Assembly approved a second four-year term for U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk.

Türk, an Austrian diplomat who has served as U.N. high commissioner for human rights since 2022, has drawn criticism from the United States and outside watchdogs over what they describe as uneven scrutiny of democracies and authoritarian governments. A 2024 analysis by UN Watch found that, among public country criticisms initiated by Türk or his office, he criticized the United States more often than China, North Korea, Cuba, Saudi Arabia and Qatar combined, while issuing no such criticism of several repressive governments during the period reviewed.

Türk’s supporters, including France and the European Union, argue that his willingness to criticize powerful democracies reflects the independence and universality required of the U.N.’s top human rights official.

France’s Geneva mission had declared that the United States was no longer a human rights leader and claimed "the world no longer listens to it" after Washington joined nine other countries in voting against Türk’s extension.

IRAN SECURES UN ROLE WITH BACKING FROM UK, FRANCE, CANADA, AUSTRALIA AS US STANDS ALONE

U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz responded by accusing France of backing an official who lectures democracies while "cozying up to the world’s worst oppressors."

Negrea went further Monday, invoking the history of the U.S.-French alliance and saying Washington had stood beside France whenever its freedom was threatened.

The United States had tolerated France’s "grandstanding" out of "a sense of camaraderie and mutual respect," he said, but would no longer remain silent in the face of what he described as feigned French "moral outrage."

Bonnafont did not directly address the walkout when he spoke again at the end of the meeting. Instead, he invoked the countries’ historic ties, noting that France helped the United States secure its independence and participated in celebrations marking America’s 250th anniversary. "This is the spirit of the relationship between France and the United States," he said, before reaffirming France’s commitment to the U.N.’s work on peace, development and human rights.

AMERICANS ARE NOT GIVING UP ON NATO, BUT THEY EXPECT EUROPE TO DO ITS SHARE

"The United Nations was created with the goal of working towards international peace and security, human rights and development," Bonnafont said, adding that France would continue working to protect the institution’s independence and its ability to serve human rights and peace.

The dispute began after the General Assembly voted 144-10, with 13 abstentions, to extend Türk’s tenure through October 2030.

The United States had unsuccessfully sought an additional week for consultations, arguing that the vote was being rushed even though Türk’s current term does not expire until Oct. 11.

Washington also objected to Türk’s record. U.S. officials have accused him of disproportionately criticizing democracies, including the United States and Israel, while failing to confront authoritarian governments with the same urgency.

item.title: A squirrel invades MLB game, jumps into outfielders glove and causes chaos in hilarious scene
item.description: Video captures a black squirrel evading 15 grounds crew members and Leody Taveras during the Orioles-Tigers game at Comerica Park on Monday night.
item.content:encoded:
Christopher Nolan’s "The Odyssey" isn’t the only long journey people are talking about, as a squirrel caused chaos at Comerica Park on Monday night.

During the bottom of the sixth inning of the Baltimore Orioles’ 8-5 win over the Detroit Tigers, a black squirrel got loose in the outfield.

The squirrel raced up and down the warning track, and play continued for a full inning while the critter made its way around the ballpark. At one point, the squirrel wasn’t too far away from a dove that was sitting on the warning track, also taking in the game.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

While the black squirrel's journey across the field may not have been as arduous as Odysseus', it was certainly entertaining.

During the top of the seventh inning, it made its way through the infield, but the game continued. The real fireworks began during the seventh-inning stretch as the grounds crew emerged to remove the squirrel.

The squirrel was making its way toward the right-field corner, and a security guard opened up the outfield gate, but the squirrel did not go through. About 15 members of the Tigers’ grounds crew, along with Orioles outfielder Leody Taveras, then tried to pick the squirrel up, but it proved elusive.

At one point, the squirrel’s shiftiness juked out one of the grounds crew so badly that it brought him to his knees.

The squirrel was chased into Taveras’ glove, but as he tried to snatch up the animal, the squirrel vaulted out of his glove and went flying before regaining his balance and continuing to flummox the grounds crew with its dexterity.

ATHLETICS' SHEA LANGELIERS, TOP MLB TRADE DEADLINE TARGET, COULD BE OUT FOR SEASON AFTER DEVASTATING INJURY

"I just was trying to stop it. When it got into my glove, I don’t want to squeeze it, so I was just trying to bring it up. I wasn’t trying to do that. But they got it out," Taveras said, via MLB.com. "I hope it’s good."

After escaping Taveras’ glove, it seemed as if the squirrel was finally trapped in the right-field corner, but it was able to dodge the towels the grounds crew threw at it and keep moving.

At one point, one member of the grounds crew was able to grab the squirrel for a moment, but it once again broke free. The squirrel dodged two attempts from the grounds crew to smother it with a towel before finally being caught under a third towel.

The grounds crew member then picked up the squirrel, which was under a towel, and was booed off the field by a vociferous Tigers’ crowd.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Play-by-play announcer Jason Benetti added some thrilling commentary as the scene unfolded.

"The chase for the squirrel is on, and the squirrel is in the corner and the squirrel is still eluding an entire horde of grounds crew members! And the squirrel is free once again, hemmed in? No! I won’t be hemmed in, I have freedom on my mind! Trying to go between the legs and eventually gets away again! And hops through the towel! And hops through another towel! The forcefield is activated, towels can’t stop him, or maybe they can," Benetti said as the squirrel was finally caught.

item.title: Costco shoppers divided over new 'sourdough' bread as critics say it's not the real thing
item.description: Costco's Kirkland olive and rosemary sourdough bread sparks heated debate over whether its long ingredient list disqualifies it as real sourdough.
item.content:encoded:
Costco's new Kirkland Signature olive and rosemary sourdough bread is a hit with many shoppers, but it's also renewed the debate about how many ingredients belong in genuine sourdough.

For bread to be labeled sourdough, it should be leavened solely with a live sourdough culture, without commercial yeast or other leavening agents, and contain no additives or other ingredients like vinegar to mimic sourdough flavor or acidity, according to the Real Bread Campaign.

"In 2015, Real Bread Campaign co-ordinator Chris Young coined the word sourfaux for any product that is named or marketed using the word sourdough, but that is made using one or more additives and/or an alternative raising agent (such as baker's yeast or baking powder) in addition to or instead of a live sourdough starter culture," the organization states on its website.

WEALTHY AMERICANS CHOOSE ONE GROCERY STORE CHAIN OVER RIVALS, SURVEY FINDS

Instagram user @costcohotfinds raved about Costco's new bread for the account's 3.5 million followers. 

"I can't stop eating this bread," @costcohotfinds creator Laura Jayne Lamb captioned her video review. "It's made with Kalamata and green olives, and it's amazing!"

She said the bread has "actual olives baked right into it," adding, "the outside is so crusty, and the center is perfectly soft and chewy."

"Please stop pushing this as sourdough," commented one Instagram user on the post. "It is not! True sourdough has flour, water and salt. Plus any inclusions. This has far too many to pass as 'sourdough.'"

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Funny you say [that], as my wife makes her own [sourdough] bread and won't buy Costco's because it has more than those three ingredients," someone replied.

"I know I was reading, the ingredients are like 50," someone else wrote, alongside a laughing emoji.

"I'll stick with making my own," commented another user.

"Support your local micro-bakeries by buying original sourdough bread from them," wrote another commenter. "Once you taste it, you can't go back to store-bought."

Sourdough purists have taken issue primarily with the Costco loaf's yeast, yeast extract and sour culture, according to Tasting Table. 

These are common ingredients in the commercial baking process, and Costco's sourdough bread is "not far off" from the real deal, the publication reported.

Costco triggered a similar discussion earlier this year when the company introduced its sourdough bread bowls. The bread bowls also contained enriched wheat flour and ingredients commonly used to speed commercial bread production, The Takeout reported.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The thing you have to remember about store-bought sourdough is that often it's not real sourdough," Kate Freebairn, an Australia-based sourdough recipe developer and author of the upcoming cookbook "Easy Sourdough On Any Schedule," told Fox News Digital. "They have still used commercial yeast."

Many social media users nevertheless agreed that the olive and rosemary bread is worth adding to their shopping carts.

"Warmed up olive and rosemary sourdough bread with a stick of butter, and I'm one happy lady," wrote one Instagram user.

"This bread is my weakness!" wrote another. "So delicious!"

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"May not be real sourdough, but it sure is delicious!" added someone else.

"Omg we get it," chimed in another Instagram user. "All the Costco bakery items have a million ingredients. No need to leave the same comment over and over in every post."

Fox News Digital reached out to Costco for comment.

item.title: Yankees vs White Sox betting preview: Gerrit Cole on the run line at +129 is tonight's play
item.description: Gerrit Cole takes the mound against Anthony Kay as the Yankees face the first-place White Sox, with the run line at +129 offering strong value.
item.content:encoded:
After a nice run, we hit a little speed bump yesterday. Last year, I felt like I was picking games poorly, but still ended up with a decent enough baseball season. This year, I think I'm doing a good job of picking games, but I'm running into some really bad luck. There are multiple games that I've lost late or had the first five lose for the full game to win (or vice versa). Things happen, but let's try to get a win here as the Yankees take on the White Sox.

Speaking of luck, it does feel like the New York Yankees are the recipients of some bad luck. When things are going right for them, they get dealt a blow like losing their annual MVP candidate, Aaron Judge. No one will feel sorry for the Yankees, but it does stink when the best players are unavailable in any sport. They have enough to get by, and few holes, even without Judge in the lineup. They do need a catcher, and they probably could benefit from a pitcher or two. We know they will be aggressive at the deadline.

Perhaps the biggest addition for them would be getting today's starter, Gerrit Cole, back to his normal performance. Cole is 3-5 for the season with a 3.92 ERA and a 1.10 WHIP. His WHIP indicates to me that he is pitching well, but might be running into some bad luck. Part of that is certainly his home runs allowed. He has given up 11 in just 62 innings this season. He has made 11 starts this season, and just three of them have been homerless outings. He has been very good against the White Sox in his career, with 10 hits allowed over 61 at-bats. He also beat them earlier this year with two earned runs in six innings.

The Chicago White Sox are likely to be in a battle for the American League Central for the remainder of this season. That's not a sentence many expected to read when the season began. They are five games over .500 and have been excellent at home this year with a 32-20 mark. Since the All-Star Break, the White Sox have gone 5-5, but they currently sit in first place in the division thanks in part to a five-game Guardians losing streak. Even if the Sox make the postseason, I think they will struggle, as they don't really have great arms in the rotation. Maybe they will trade for someone.

Speaking of their rotation, tonight's starter, Anthony Kay, looks to lead them to victory. Kay has been fine for them with a 7-4 record and a 4.21 ERA, and a 1.37 WHIP. None of those numbers are overly impressive. Kay has been significantly better in home starts, throwing to a 3.06 ERA. That's 2.50 lower than his road ERA. He faced the Yankees earlier this season and allowed four earned runs on six hits in four innings of work.

The Yankees are slightly below league average for batting against left-handed pitchers. They have a .239 batting average against lefties, but they do have the better pitcher. If Cole can keep the ball in the yard, he should be able to get the Yankees a win. The White Sox are very homer-dependent and rank 7th in home runs.

There aren't going to be a ton of times where you can get Cole at a reasonable number, and today is one of those days. I know Kay has been better at home, and the line is moving in favor of the White Sox, but the Yankees are the better team and have the better pitcher and bullpen. I'm taking them on the run line at +129. If you want the safer option, the moneyline is -131.
